title: Math Notes
text:
0.1 Goal
A personal math wiki. One concept per day, 30–60 minutes, written by hand first and then transferred to a .qmd file here.
Build measure-theoretic probability fluency the long way around: linear algebra fluency first (Axler), then real analysis (Abbott), then probability proper (Rosenthal). Parallel tracks (Needham, Strogatz, Mahajan) keep the geometric and physical instincts alive on lower-energy days.

title: Math Notes
text:
0.2 Workflow

Session — 30–45 min on paper. Read the concept. Work an example. Draw the diagram. Write the definition in your own words. The friction is the point.
Transfer — 15–20 min later. Open a new .qmd from _templates/concept.qmd. Fill in Statement → Intuition → Example → Counterexample → Connection to work. The template surfaces what you don’t yet understand.
Photograph the notebook page and drop it in notebook/. Embed alongside the typeset version.

A few hours of delay between handwriting and typing is better than back-to-back — the slight forgetting pressure is useful.

title: Math Notes
text:
0.3 Cadence

Mon–Thu — primary text, one concept per day
Fri — Needham (or another parallel track)
Sat — synthesis note for the week
Sun — off

See Schedule for the 60-week plan and each phase for the concept list.

2.1 Daily routine
60 weeks, ~5 sessions/week. Start: Mon 2026-06-01. End: Sun 2027-07-25.
The schedule is a target, not a contract. Real life slips; the right response is to shift the calendar, not to skip the daily handwriting session. Fluency, not speed.

title: 2  Schedule
text:
2.6 Parallel tracks
Run alongside the phase work, no fixed schedule beyond “Friday by default.”

Needham — Visual Complex Analysis. Chs 1–5 to start. Geometric instinct, low activation energy.
Osgood — Lectures on the Fourier Transform and Its Applications. Stanford EE 261. Intuition + rigor, signal-processing applications, distributions and sampling. Friday substitute when Needham isn’t pulling.
Strogatz — Nonlinear Dynamics and Chaos. Browse-driven; pick a chapter when curious.
Mahajan — Street-Fighting Mathematics. One problem per low-energy session. Counterweight to formalism.

title: 3  Linear Algebra — Axler
text:
3.1 Concepts
Primary text. Sheldon Axler, Linear Algebra Done Right.
Companions. Strang (Introduction to Linear Algebra) for geometric matrix pictures; Lang (Linear Algebra) for the algebraic generalization over arbitrary fields.
Phase window. 2026-06-01 → 2026-09-13. ~15 weeks (~3.5 months).
Why first. Axler formalizes what’s already intuitive from applied work (Cholesky, covariance geometry, eigendecompositions). Familiar ground means lower cognitive load, which is the right shape for establishing the daily habit before analysis gets genuinely hard.
Append as you go. Numbering is for ordering, not for hierarchy.

title: 4  Real Analysis — Abbott
text:
4.1 Concepts
Primary text. Stephen Abbott, Understanding Analysis.
Phase window. 2026-09-14 → 2027-01-31. ~20 weeks (~5 months).
Why. Builds the ε–δ and limit machinery that Rosenthal assumes for measure-theoretic probability. Abbott is rigorous but intuition-first; not punishing.

title: 5  Measure-Theoretic Probability — Rosenthal
text:
5.1 Concepts
Primary text. Jeffrey Rosenthal, A First Look at Rigorous Probability Theory.
Phase window. 2027-02-01 → 2027-07-25. ~25 weeks (~6 months).
Why. The original target of this whole effort. Direct payoff for Bayesian modeling (posteriors as conditional expectations, Radon-Nikodym as likelihoods), sequential trial design (martingales, optional stopping), and limit theorems used routinely without their measure-theoretic justification.

5.2 After Phase 3
Two natural continuations, choose at the time:

Martingales → Williams, Probability with Martingales. Optional stopping, sequential trials.
Radon-Nikodym → densities, likelihoods, change of measure. Direct line back to Bayesian inference.

title: 6  Complex Analysis — Needham
text:
6.1 Concepts
Text. Tristan Needham, Visual Complex Analysis.
Mode. Friday parallel track. Chs 1–5 to start (geometry of complex functions, Möbius transformations, differentiation as amplitwist).
Why. Keeps the geometric instinct alive while the primary phase is heads-down on proofs. Needham is the manifesto for intuition-over-symbol-pushing; perfect Friday material.

title: 7  Fourier Analysis — Osgood
text:
7.1 Concepts
Text. Brad Osgood, Lectures on the Fourier Transform and Its Applications (Stanford EE 261 notes).
Mode. Parallel track. Self-paced; pick a chapter when a phase week feels heavy, or use as a Friday substitute when Needham isn’t pulling.
Why. Osgood’s lectures are the rare text that gives both the intuition (heat equation, signal processing, the symmetry between time and frequency) and the rigor (distributions, Schwartz class, sampling theorem). Geometric and applied — a natural fit alongside Needham. Direct connections to deconvolution, frequency-domain identification, and any time-series work in PK/PD.

title: 8  Nonlinear Dynamics — Strogatz
text:
8.1 Concepts
Text. Steven Strogatz, Nonlinear Dynamics and Chaos.
Mode. Browse-driven; low-energy day substitute for the primary text. Pick a chapter when curious — fixed points, bifurcations, phase portraits, chaos.
Why. Physical intuition for dynamical systems; counterweight to pure formalism. Many concepts (stability, attractors, sensitivity) translate directly into how to read PK/PD and ODE-driven models.

title: 9  Estimation — Mahajan
text:
9.1 Problems
Text. Sanjoy Mahajan, Street-Fighting Mathematics.
Mode. Practice mode, not a sequential curriculum. One problem per low-energy session. Dimensional analysis, easy cases, lumping, pictorial proofs, taking out the big part.
Why. Estimation is its own cognitive exercise — different from a Rosenthal proof and valuable for exactly that reason. 30 minutes on a Mahajan problem keeps the useful approximation muscle in shape.
